title: The billing emails that lost money
scenario:
You are a business analyst at an energy supplier. The customer team gets about 20,000 billing questions by email each month. A two-week pilot let an AI assistant answer a sample of them directly.

The pilot team says: "76% of answers were correct. That's a great result, let's roll it out." The finance director asks you to check the business case before she signs. The exhibit shows the value model and the pilot results.
exhibit:
Billing emails: value model and pilot (made-up example data)

Value per email
  AI answers correctly       saves 5 EUR of agent time
  AI answers wrongly         customer calls back, complaint work:
                             costs 20 EUR
  AI hands off to an agent   costs 1 EUR (agent reads the AI note)

Pilot result (1,000 emails, no hand-off rule)
  Correct   760
  Wrong     240

Draft business case, running cost line:
  "Model cost: tiny, not worth estimating."

questions.prompt: Using the value model, what does the pilot result mean?

options.text: The pilot is a clear success, because 76% correct is well above half of all emails.
options.explanation: "Above half" is not the test. The test is whether savings beat the cost of failures, and here they don't.

options.text: The result can't be judged at all until the system has run for a full year.
options.explanation: The value model already lets you judge it: you can compare savings with the cost of failures now.

options.text: The design loses money: 760 × 5 EUR is less than 240 × 20 EUR, and break-even is 80%.
options.explanation: Right. 3,800 EUR saved against 4,800 EUR in failure costs. As in OpenAI's guide, the break-even accuracy is the number that decides.

options.text: The design saves money, because each correct answer saves time and most answers are correct.
options.explanation: Each wrong answer costs four times what a correct one saves. Most correct is not enough at these values.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with the running-cost line in the draft?

options.text: Nothing. Model costs are always too small to matter in a business case for email.
options.explanation: At 20,000 emails a month, cost depends on volume and prices. You can't know it is small without estimating it.

options.text: It should list the most expensive model's price, so that the case is safe in any situation.
options.explanation: A worst-case guess is not an estimate. Use the model you plan to run and its real token use.

options.text: It should be replaced with the vendor's marketing claim about how much AI usually saves.
options.explanation: A general claim doesn't describe your volume, your tokens or your prices.

options.text: It needs tokens × price per token, with the price page and date, plus people costs.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's production guide frames cost as tokens times cost per token. Name the price page and the date so others can check it, and add review and maintenance time.

questions.prompt: The pilot team never measured the current process. Which baseline matters most for this case?

options.text: Today's handling time, cost per email and share of correct answers by agents.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic's ticket routing guide lists criteria like these that apply with or without an LLM. Without them, you can't show a gain.

options.text: The number of AI tools the competitors use for their billing emails.
options.explanation: That says nothing about your own process, so it can't show whether you gained anything.

options.text: The total number of emails the company has received over the last ten years or more.
options.explanation: Old volume doesn't tell you today's time, cost or quality per email.

options.text: How many staff members said they liked the AI during the two-week pilot.
options.explanation: Staff opinion is useful, but it is not a baseline for time, cost or correct answers.

questions.prompt: How could the design change so that the case becomes positive?

options.text: Answer every email with AI, so that the volume of savings grows large enough to cover the losses.
options.explanation: At 76% correct, each email loses money on average. More volume makes the loss bigger, not smaller.

options.text: Hand off to an agent when the model isn't sure, so many costly wrong answers become 1 EUR hand-offs.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's guide lists handing off to a person when the intent is unclear. A hand-off costs 1 EUR here; a wrong answer costs 20 EUR.

options.text: Remove the cost of wrong answers from the model, since complaints are handled by another team anyway.
options.explanation: The cost is real even if another budget pays it. Hiding it makes the case look better on paper only.

options.text: Report 76% as the success rate and leave out the failure costs, since finance only asks for accuracy.
options.explanation: The finance director asked for the business case. Leaving out failure costs gives her the wrong answer.
